gamiDialog.dashboardCelebrate1: All of today's missions are done. The rest of the day is yours — enjoy it calmly.
gamiDialog.dashboardCelebrate2: Your missions are complete. Rest is part of recovery too.
gamiDialog.dashboardGentle1: Today feels heavy, and you still showed up. That is already a step.
gamiDialog.dashboardGentle2: It's okay, you are not alone — I'm here with you today.
gamiDialog.dashboardWave2: Hello again! One small step today is enough.
gamiDialog.m1High1: A strong urge on a hard day is the toughest combination. You don't have to fight it alone — let's get through these few minutes together.
gamiDialog.m1High2: When everything feels heavy at once, one small step is enough. Support is always open to you, too.
gamiDialog.m1Low1: A heavy day with a small urge alongside it. That's okay — urges usually fade on their own within minutes.
gamiDialog.m1Low2: You are carrying a lot right now. Give yourself a small pause; I'm right here with you.
gamiDialog.m1None1: Thank you for being honest about your day. No urge today — one thing you don't have to think about right now.
gamiDialog.m1None2: A heavy day is still worth recording. You showed up, and that is not a small thing.
gamiDialog.m2High1: Anxiety plus a strong urge is exhausting. Remember: an urge is a wave — the peak is brief, then it falls.
gamiDialog.m2High2: When you're anxious, urges can feel louder than usual. You have gotten through this before; you can this time too.
gamiDialog.m2Low1: A hard day, and a small urge came along. That's normal; urges usually settle on their own within minutes.
gamiDialog.m2Low2: Anxiety and urges often arrive together. Both will pass — slow breathing helps them along.
gamiDialog.m2None1: Anxious but no urge means you are facing your day, not the old habit. That is real progress.
gamiDialog.m2None2: Thank you for noting your anxiety. Naming a feeling is how you slow it down.
gamiDialog.m3High1: Your mood is neutral but the urge feels strong. That happens — urges don't always follow mood. A short pause can help.
gamiDialog.m3High2: Strong urges can appear even on flat days. You noticed it early — that is your advantage.
gamiDialog.m3Low1: A neutral day with a small urge — a good moment for a short practice while everything is still light.
gamiDialog.m3Low2: A small urge on an ordinary day is normal. Recording it like this keeps it small.
gamiDialog.m3None1: An ordinary day is worth recording too. You showed up for yourself, and that is enough.
gamiDialog.m3None2: Not every day has to be special. Being quietly present like this is a good foundation.
gamiDialog.m4High1: You are calm but the urge is strong — actually the best time to practice, because you are still in control.
gamiDialog.m4High2: A strong urge doesn't always mean danger; it means your body is remembering an old pattern. You decide the next step.
gamiDialog.m4Low1: You are fairly calm even with a small urge around. You are proving your response can be chosen.
gamiDialog.m4Low2: Calm and still aware — a good combination. This small urge will pass.
gamiDialog.m4None1: Calm and no urge. Hold on to how this feels — this is what you are building.
gamiDialog.m4None2: Calm like this is the result of your small steps. Enjoy it.
gamiDialog.m5High1: Glad your day feels good. Urges sometimes arrive exactly when you relax — that's okay, you know how to pause.
gamiDialog.m5High2: A good day with a strong urge is deceptive — stay a little aware, but don't let it spoil your day.
gamiDialog.m5Low1: Your day is good and the urge is small. You are in a strong position to let it pass.
gamiDialog.m5Low2: Feeling good and a small urge can coexist. You don't have to react at all.
gamiDialog.m5None1: A good day with no urge — enjoy it, and remember what made it this way.
gamiDialog.m5None2: Glad your day is going well. Notes like this help you learn the recipe for your good days.

mythFact.title: Myth or fact?
mythFact.resultWrong: Not quite — this one is a {answer}.
mythFact.mf1Statement: A site that hasn't paid out for a while is bound to 'run hot' soon.
mythFact.mf1Explanation: Every round stands alone and remembers nothing before it. 'Running hot' is a story built to keep people playing.
mythFact.mf2Statement: In the long run, online gambling is set up so players lose.
mythFact.mf2Explanation: Every game carries a mathematical edge for the house. The longer you play, the more certain the total loss.
mythFact.mf3Statement: Almost winning means you are getting closer to a win.
mythFact.mf3Explanation: Near-misses are designed to make the brain feel it almost succeeded, while the odds never changed. The effect makes people play longer.
mythFact.mf4Statement: The best way to recover losses is to keep playing until you break even.
mythFact.mf4Explanation: Chasing losses is the pattern that most reliably deepens them. Stopping is the only step that actually stops the minus.
mythFact.mf5Statement: A lucky streak does not change the odds of the next bet.
mythFact.mf5Explanation: Winning streaks feel like a pattern, but each bet's odds stay the same. The 'hot hand' feeling is a mental bias, not mathematics.
mythFact.mf6Statement: While gambling, people often lose their sense of time without noticing.
mythFact.mf6Explanation: Games deliberately remove time cues so sessions feel short. That is why an outside time limit helps so much.
mythFact.mf7Statement: With enough skill, online slots can be beaten.
mythFact.mf7Explanation: Slot outcomes come from a random number generator, not skill. No technique changes the odds.
mythFact.mf8Statement: Easy early wins are part of the design to hook new players.
mythFact.mf8Explanation: Bonuses and early wins teach the brain to tag gambling as rewarding. Once hooked, the pattern of bigger bets begins.
mythFact.mf9Statement: After many losses, a win must be getting closer.
mythFact.mf9Explanation: Odds have no memory; a long losing run makes no win 'due'. This belief is known as the gambler's fallacy.
mythFact.mf10Statement: A gambling urge fades on its own even if you don't act on it.
mythFact.mf10Explanation: Urges work like waves: they rise, peak, and fall within minutes. Riding one out makes the next wave smaller.
mythFact.mf11Statement: Small bets are harmless because the money is small.
mythFact.mf11Explanation: The danger is not the first amount but the pattern it builds. Small bets are an entry door designed to feel safe.
mythFact.mf12Statement: Gambling ads only show winners' stories, not the average player's reality.
mythFact.mf12Explanation: Winning stories are selected and paid to appear; millions of losses are never advertised. What you see is curation, not data.
mythFact.mf13Statement: Borrowing money to play just once is fine as long as you pay it back quickly.
mythFact.mf13Explanation: Borrowing to gamble is the most serious warning sign and almost always repeats. When this thought appears, that is the moment to reach for support.
mythFact.mf14Statement: Gambling triggers can be recognized and mapped.
mythFact.mf14Explanation: Most urges follow patterns: certain hours, boredom, stress, or notifications. Knowing your triggers lets you prepare a response.
mythFact.mf15Statement: Needing a blocking app means your willpower is weak.
mythFact.mf15Explanation: Shaping your environment is the most effective self-control strategy in research. People who recover use every tool available.
mythFact.mf16Statement: Removing triggers from your environment beats willpower alone.
mythFact.mf16Explanation: Willpower is limited and drains when you are tired. A designed environment works even in your weakest moments.
mythFact.mf17Statement: One more round can help fix a bad mood.
mythFact.mf17Explanation: Gambling to repair feelings strengthens the cycle: after losing, you feel worse. What actually works is movement, breathing, or talking to someone.
mythFact.mf18Statement: Lack of sleep makes urges harder to control.
mythFact.mf18Explanation: Sleep restores the brain's impulse brakes. Even one short night lowers self-control the next day.
mythFact.mf19Statement: Only weak people get addicted to online gambling.
mythFact.mf19Explanation: Online gambling is engineered by expert teams to hook any brain, clever or not. Addiction is a brain's response to that design, not a character flaw.
mythFact.mf20Statement: Naming the feeling you are having lowers its intensity.
mythFact.mf20Explanation: Saying 'I am anxious' shifts brain activity from the alarm center to the language center. The effect is measurable: intensity drops.
mythFact.mf21Statement: Winning your money back proves you are still in control.
mythFact.mf21Explanation: Breaking even is the story the brain uses to continue the pattern. Real control is the ability not to start.
mythFact.mf22Statement: Unpredictable rewards hook the brain more than certain ones.
mythFact.mf22Explanation: This is the core mechanism of gambling machines: variable rewards trigger the strongest dopamine response. Social media uses the same mechanism.
mythFact.mf23Statement: Lucky charms or rituals can improve your odds.
mythFact.mf23Explanation: Odds are set by the system, not rituals. Charm beliefs create an illusion of control — which makes people play longer.
mythFact.mf24Statement: Support from others speeds up recovery from gambling.
mythFact.mf24Explanation: Accompanied recovery lasts longer than going alone. Talking to one trusted person already changes your odds.
mythFact.mf25Statement: Online gambling is fairer than offline because a computer runs it.
mythFact.mf25Explanation: Online systems can tune odds more finely and without oversight. 'Run by computer' means run for the owner's profit.
mythFact.mf26Statement: One slip does not mean your recovery failed.
mythFact.mf26Explanation: Lapses are a common part of quitting, not the end of it. What matters is the next step, not the slip.
mythFact.mf27Statement: Watching gambling content is harmless as long as you don't play.
mythFact.mf27Explanation: Watching activates the same reward circuits and normalizes the habit. It is the most common way old urges reignite.
mythFact.mf28Statement: Money limits work best when set before temptation arrives.
mythFact.mf28Explanation: Decisions made while calm are stronger than ones made while triggered. That is why limits and blockers are set in advance.
mythFact.mf29Statement: Quitting gambling should be done alone so it really counts.
mythFact.mf29Explanation: There is no evidence that going alone strengthens recovery — isolation raises relapse risk. Asking for help is strategy, not weakness.
mythFact.mf30Statement: Boredom is one of the most common gambling triggers.
mythFact.mf30Explanation: Gambling sessions most often start not from wanting money but from having nothing to do. A ready list of boredom-fillers is a real defense.

quickQuiz.title: Quick quiz
quickQuiz.intro: Three short questions to refresh what you've learned.
quickQuiz.doneBody: Recalling like this strengthens what you know. New questions arrive tomorrow.
quickQuiz.qq1Question: How long does the peak of a gambling urge usually last?
quickQuiz.qq1Explanation: Urges work like waves: they rise, peak for a few minutes, then fall on their own — even without acting on them.
quickQuiz.qq2Question: What does a 10-second pause before acting do?
quickQuiz.qq2Choice1: Gives the brain room to choose a response
quickQuiz.qq2Explanation: A short pause moves control from reflex to consideration. Urges lose much of their power in those seconds.
quickQuiz.qq3Question: What is the effect of naming a feeling ('I am anxious')?
quickQuiz.qq3Explanation: Naming an emotion activates the brain's language center and calms its alarm center — a measurable research effect.
quickQuiz.qq4Question: Which self-control strategy does research rank most effective?
quickQuiz.qq4Choice2: Designing your environment so triggers stay away
quickQuiz.qq4Explanation: Willpower drains quickly; environments work continuously. Removing triggers makes the healthy choice the easiest choice.
quickQuiz.qq5Question: How does sleep relate to self-control?
quickQuiz.qq5Choice1: Lack of sleep weakens the brain's impulse brakes
quickQuiz.qq5Choice2: Sleep has nothing to do with urges
quickQuiz.qq5Explanation: The brain's impulse brakes recover during sleep. Even one short night lowers self-control the next day.
quickQuiz.qq6Question: What does 'house edge' mean in online gambling?
quickQuiz.qq6Choice3: The operator's mathematical advantage in every game
quickQuiz.qq6Explanation: Every game is mathematically tilted toward the operator. The longer you play, the more certain the total loss.
quickQuiz.qq7Question: Why does 'almost winning' feel so compelling?
quickQuiz.qq7Choice1: Because a win really is close
quickQuiz.qq7Choice2: Because the brain tags it like near-success, though odds never changed
quickQuiz.qq7Choice3: Because the system gives consolation prizes
quickQuiz.qq7Explanation: Near-misses fire the reward circuit as if you almost succeeded. The odds never moved — the design makes you want to continue.
quickQuiz.qq8Question: What is the best response after losing a bet?
quickQuiz.qq8Choice1: Stop — continuing almost certainly deepens the loss
quickQuiz.qq8Choice2: Raise the stake to win it back faster
quickQuiz.qq8Explanation: Chasing losses is the most destructive pattern. The only way to stop the minus is to stop playing.
quickQuiz.qq9Question: Which kind of intention is easiest to live by?
quickQuiz.qq9Choice1: A grand vow like 'I will totally change'
quickQuiz.qq9Choice2: A promise to never fail again
quickQuiz.qq9Choice3: A small specific intention like 'laptop closed at 9'
quickQuiz.qq9Explanation: Small concrete intentions can be acted on and measured immediately. Grand vows without a first step collapse easily.
quickQuiz.qq10Question: What is the purpose of the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding practice?
quickQuiz.qq10Choice2: Returning attention to the body and the present moment
quickQuiz.qq10Explanation: Grounding pulls attention out of spiraling thoughts into the senses: what you see, touch, hear. The body settles, the mind follows.
quickQuiz.qq11Question: Which condition most often starts a gambling session?
quickQuiz.qq11Explanation: Most sessions start not from wanting money but from empty time. A ready list of alternatives is a real defense.
quickQuiz.qq12Question: Why do random rewards hook harder than certain ones?
quickQuiz.qq12Choice3: Because unpredictability triggers the strongest dopamine
quickQuiz.qq12Explanation: Unpredictable rewards are the core mechanism of gambling machines — and social media. The brain keeps trying 'one more time'.
quickQuiz.qq13Question: What is the best step after a single slip?
quickQuiz.qq13Choice1: Declare the recovery a total failure
quickQuiz.qq13Choice2: Return to the recovery routine without self-punishment
quickQuiz.qq13Explanation: Lapses are a normal part of quitting. What matters is the next step — not the slip.
quickQuiz.qq14Question: When is the best time to set money and time limits?
quickQuiz.qq14Explanation: Decisions made while calm are stronger than ones made while triggered. That is why limits and blockers are set in advance.
quickQuiz.qq15Question: What role does other people's support play in recovery?
quickQuiz.qq15Choice1: It makes recovery feel less proven
quickQuiz.qq15Choice2: It is only needed for severe cases
quickQuiz.qq15Choice3: It speeds up and strengthens recovery
quickQuiz.qq15Explanation: Accompanied recovery lasts longer. Talking to one trusted person already changes your odds.

estimator.title: What you kept
estimator.setupBody: Estimate your old habit: roughly how many hours and how much money per week it used to take. These numbers stay in this browser only and are never sent anywhere.
estimator.savedIntro: Across {days} active days in the last {range} days, an estimate of what stayed with you:
estimator.approxNote: This is a rough estimate from your own baseline, not a transaction record. Its value is the direction, not the digits.
estimator.empowerLine: This time and money remain yours — for things you choose yourself.

weeklyRecap.title: Your week's story

card.activeDays: days you showed up this week

weeklyRecap.recapStrong: A week full of presence. A rhythm like this is what real recovery is built on.
weeklyRecap.recapSteady: You kept coming back this week, and that is what matters most. Rhythm is built from presence, not perfection.
weeklyRecap.recapGentle: This week felt heavy, and you are still here. Showing up is itself a step.

scenarioSim.title: How would you respond?
scenarioSim.fictionalNote: Fictional scenarios for practicing replies. No scores, nothing is sent.
scenarioSim.doneBody: A line you have rehearsed comes out far more easily when the real moment arrives.

friend_invite.intro: “Bro, this new site is going wild. Come on, tiny stake, just for fun.”
friend_invite.prompt: Your friend is inviting you. What do you say?
friend_invite.choice1: “No, I've quit. 'Going wild' or 'running hot' is just a trick to keep people playing.”
friend_invite.choice2: “Fine, just this once. It's small anyway.”
friend_invite.outcome1: Clear, firm, no drama. Naming the reason makes your refusal hard to argue with — invitations usually stop after two refusals like this.
friend_invite.outcome2: “Just once” is the classic entry door — almost every relapse starts with this sentence. Try again and feel the difference of refusing outright.
friend_invite.outcome3: Delaying is a valid tactic and often works. If the invitation returns, the assertive script closes the door for good.

judol_ad.intro: An ad appears in your feed: a creator flashes a balance and says “50 thousand became 5 million, hurry before you miss out!”
judol_ad.choice1: Get curious and open the link briefly, just to look.
judol_ad.choice2: Close it, block the account, and report the ad.
judol_ad.outcome1: “Just looking” is how the old circuit relights — the page is designed to turn looking into trying. Try again: which step closes the door?
judol_ad.outcome2: The strongest move: you didn't just avoid it, you removed the bait from your future feed. That flashed balance is curation, not reality.
judol_ad.outcome3: Scrolling past saved you today. If similar ads keep coming, block and report stops them more permanently.

pinjol.intro: End of the month, money is thin. A thought passes: “borrow 200 thousand in an app, play a little, I can repay it before it's due.”
pinjol.prompt: That thought appears. How do you respond?
pinjol.choice1: Postpone it: “I'll think about it tomorrow.”
pinjol.choice2: Download the app “just to check the limit.”
pinjol.choice3: Recognize this as a serious signal and contact someone you trust now.
pinjol.outcome1: Postponing gives the urge time to fade — that is valuable. But a loan-to-play thought is the most serious signal; tell someone today as well.
pinjol.outcome2: “Checking the limit” is step one of a fast-moving chain: download, register, disburse, gone. Try again — which response breaks the chain earlier?
pinjol.outcome3: This is the strongest response. Borrowing to play is the number-one danger sign, and telling someone right away is the surest way to stop it.
